It is the fifth set of the 2023 Wimbledon final. Carlos Alcaraz, twenty years old, is serving for the biggest title of his life. Novak Djokovic, 23-time Grand Slam champion, stands across the net. The stadium is unanimous: something has shifted. The momentum, every pundit agrees, belongs to Alcaraz now.

He went on to win. The narrative wrote itself.

But did winning under that kind of pressure actually make the next points more likely to go his way? Or did fifteen thousand people in the stands just fall for one of sport's oldest statistical traps?

Gilovich et al. (1985) famously dismissed the "hot hand" as a cognitive illusion. However, Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) later proved this analysis contained a streak selection bias that systematically underestimated genuine persistence. In tennis, recent CUSUM-based studies (tracking cumulative performance deviations) like Du et al. (2025) find traces of momentum, but rely on thin 31-match samples measuring correlation, not cause.

This project scales the test entirely. I analysed 52,314 points across all four 2023 Grand Slams on both the ATP and WTA tours, seven times the size of the most recent study. The results suggest momentum in tennis is highly context-dependent, reversing sign across pressure situations.

The raw data comes from Jeff Sackmann's Match Charting Project, a publicly available volunteer-compiled database where tennis analysts manually record every point played in professional matches, including the exact score state at each moment. As a volunteer-compiled database, marginal human input error is possible, though the scale of 52,314 observations substantially mitigates the impact of random data-entry errors. The same dataset has been used in prior momentum research, including Du et al. (2025); the contribution here is scale and the break point vs tiebreak distinction. This allowed me to identify high-pressure situations with precision: break points (where the returner is one point from winning the game) and tiebreaks (where a set hangs in the balance). I defined these as high-leverage moments, a category combining break points (13.5% of all points) and tiebreak points (3.5%). Across the ATP tour, 17% of points were high-leverage; across the WTA, 16%.

The dataset covers 35,635 ATP points (155 matches) and 16,679 WTA points (120 matches), reflecting the men's best-of-five format.

Data was standardised by matching player records and excluding retirements and qualifying rounds. I used official ATP and WTA rankings to measure baseline skill, consistent with Kovalchik (2016). Rankings were chosen over Elo because a two-stage matching process, using tournament-specific rankings with season-average fallback, achieved full coverage across all 52,314 points.

I kept the tours separate throughout, since pooling them would have obscured the comparison that matters most.

## Does Momentum Even Show Up in the Data?

Does winning a point make the next one more likely to go your way?

I ran two tests for every player individually: a Pearson Chi-squared independence test and a Wald-Wolfowitz runs test. The Chi-squared test asks whether point outcomes are independent; the runs test asks whether wins and losses cluster beyond chance. I tested 77 ATP players and 78 WTA players separately, rather than pooling everyone. Pooling would risk hiding individual patterns inside aggregate noise.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output1_chi2_table.html" width="100%" height="180" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The results are the first blow to the momentum theory. In the ATP, 10.4% of players showed statistical evidence that their point sequences were non-random on the Chi-squared test, and 13.0% on the runs test. In the WTA, the figures are lower still: 6.4% and 9.0%. After applying a Benjamini-Hochberg correction to control the false discovery rate (the proportion of flagged results that are actually false alarms) across all players, zero remain significant on the Chi-squared test in either tour, and only one per tour survives on the runs test. The uncorrected figures barely exceeded the 5% random baseline; once adjusted, evidence for individual momentum vanishes.

But I cannot stop here. As Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) mathematically proved, traditional methods like the runs test are notoriously underpowered, meaning they will often miss real effects that genuinely exist, and are systematically biased against finding momentum in short sequences.

The chart below tracks the cumulative momentum score across the longest WTA match in the dataset. The line rises when the player wins above her average rate and falls when she drops below. Genuine momentum would look like a staircase, not a weather chart.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output2_cusum_wta.html" width="100%" height="420" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The chart shows a sustained above-average run that eventually collapses. The line spends the first 150 points predominantly above zero, suggesting Alexandrova is controlling the match, before dropping sharply from around point 180 to its lowest point at 187. There is no sustained directional run anywhere. Du et al. (2025) argue that this kind of oscillation is itself evidence of momentum shifting between players. I read it differently: it looks like the natural variance of two evenly matched competitors trading points.

## What About the Biggest Moments?

For every player, I calculated their Tiebreak Over-Expectation (TBOE): their actual tiebreak win rate minus their predicted win rate based on official ranking and recent form. If certain players consistently raise their game when it matters most, I would expect to see clear outliers pulling sharply away from zero in either direction.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output3_tboe_scatter.html" width="100%" height="460" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The chart plots TBOE scores for players with at least 20 tiebreak points, from lowest to highest, to prevent finite-sample variance from creating artificial outliers (Miller and Sanjurjo, 2018). Of the full sample, 23 ATP players and 6 WTA players qualify. In the ATP, the distribution runs gradually from Milos Raonic at -0.11 to Holger Rune at +0.07, with no player pulling sharply away from the pack. The WTA sample is too small to draw strong conclusions: only 6 players qualify, and Martina Trevisan at +0.26 sits visually apart, though this likely reflects the limited sample rather than genuine clutch ability.

## Correlation or Causation?

Everything so far has tested whether momentum correlates with winning the next point. But correlation is not causation. A player who is already dominating will naturally win more break points. The association might simply reflect that good players win more of everything, not that winning one big point is responsible for winning the next.

I use a causal forest to estimate whether winning a pressure point causes a higher probability of winning the next. Unlike standard regression, which assumes identical effects for everyone, the causal forest estimates heterogeneous effects. It splits the data into subgroups and estimates the effect, using sample-splitting to prevent overfitting and spurious pattern matching. The key assumption is that controlling for the four control variables captures all systematic differences between players who win and lose high-leverage points, with no hidden factor simultaneously driving the pressure outcome and the next point.

I define a high-leverage win as a point where the player faced a break point or tiebreak situation and won it, consistent with Gilovich et al. (1985) and Miller and Sanjurjo (2018), who both define momentum as success breeding success, not merely exposure to pressure. Restricting the control group to lost pressure points was rejected because, in tiebreaks, the alternating serve structure can mechanically disadvantage the point winner on the next point. The baseline therefore comprises all other match points.

The model holds four variables constant to isolate the pressure point effect: player ranking, rolling win percentage over the last ten points, winning streak length over the last four points, and cumulative momentum score. A Bayesian prior (a starting estimate that updates as evidence accumulates) of 0.38 (the tour-wide return win rate) anchors initial break point expectations. Standard errors are clustered by match, since points within the same match are not independent. To avoid double-counting zero-sum points, one focal player is randomly selected per match and all observations are tracked from their perspective. A Variance Inflation Factor check confirmed no multicollinearity among the baseline predictors, with all VIF scores below 1.2. Early-match points are included as CUSUM volatility is lower, not higher, at match start.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output4_cate_plot.html" width="100%" height="460" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The first chart shows the estimated causal effect broken down by player ranking band. Across all four bands in both tours, the effect sits below zero. Top-ranked players show no meaningful positive momentum effect. Neither do qualifiers.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output5_model_table.html" width="100%" height="540" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The second chart breaks this down by variable. Two findings stand out. First, the Break Point Win row sits left of zero in both tours, while the Tiebreak Win row sits right of zero, previewing the finding explored in the next section. Second, rolling win percentage behaves in completely opposite directions between tours: negative for ATP and positive for WTA, though the WTA error bar is wide, making the estimate imprecise. This suggests recent form plays a meaningfully different role in women's tennis than in men's, a tour-specific pattern that would have been invisible if the two datasets had been merged. Player rank and the other control rows sit close to zero across both tours, suggesting baseline skill level alone does not determine who wins the next point.

The combined causal effect is negative for both tours (ATP: -0.0325, WTA: -0.0363). The combined WTA estimate is more negative than the break point estimate alone. This reflects Simpson's Paradox: pooling break points and tiebreaks changes the composition of the treatment group and can reverse the aggregate pattern relative to the subgroup results.

If I stopped here, the hot hand would look like a fallacy. But this combined number treats all high-leverage moments as identical. What happens if I split the two types of pressure apart?

## The Finding That Changes Everything


::: {.reveal-section}
<div class="reveal-chart" id="reveal-chart"></div>
:::

<div class="reveal-controls">
<button class="reveal-btn active" data-view="combined">Combined Effect</button>
<button class="reveal-btn" data-view="split">Split by Pressure Type</button>
</div>

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![The combined null effect breaks into two opposite effects when break points and tiebreaks are separated.](outputs/output5_model_table.png)
:::

As the chart shows, converting a break point is associated with a reduced probability of winning the next point in both tours. Break points appear to generate a clear, measurable drag. Tiebreaks tell the opposite story. The ATP estimate (+0.0564) is the chart's dominant feature, comparable in magnitude to the break point hangover and opposite in sign. The WTA effect (+0.0209) is consistent in direction, statistically significant (p=0.0006, 95% CI: 0.009 to 0.033), and smaller in magnitude, reflecting the limited 197-observation sample.

This explains why the combined number is negative. Break points are far more common than tiebreaks: 13.5% of all ATP points are break points, compared to just 3.5% in tiebreaks. The hangover effect happens more often, so it dominates the aggregate. When all high-leverage moments are treated as identical, the tiebreak momentum signal gets buried.

## If Not Momentum, Then What?

Outside of tiebreaks, if momentum does not drive point outcomes, what does? The chart below ranks the four variables by how much each one drives variation in the causal effect.

```{=html}
<div style="border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; margin:1.5rem 0;">
<iframe src="outputs/output7_feature_importance.html" width="100%" height="420" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>
```

The cumulative momentum score dominates everything else. In the ATP, it accounts for 0.50 of the variance in the treatment effect, significantly ahead of player rank at 0.32 and rolling win percentage at 0.16. In the WTA, the pattern holds: momentum score at 0.52, player rank at 0.28, rolling win percentage at 0.19.

The most striking feature of the chart is the bar you can barely see. Winning Streak, which measures whether a player won their last four consecutive points, scores 0.024 in the ATP and 0.010 in the WTA. It is virtually flat. Knowing that a player is on a short hot streak tells the model almost nothing once the cumulative trajectory is accounted for. The hot hand, in its most literal form, has no predictive power here.

What shapes the momentum effect most is accumulated match drift, not short-term bursts of form.

## The Uncomfortable Conclusion

Within this sample, momentum in tennis is not universal. It operates in opposite directions depending on context. Winning a break point is estimated to reduce the probability of winning the next point by around 6 percentage points in the ATP and 3 in the WTA. Winning a tiebreak point is estimated to increase it. The break point effect is a hangover, the opposite of what every commentator assumes. The tiebreak effect is consistent with positive momentum, exactly the kind of carryover crowds imagine, but only in that context. These two effects, opposite in sign, can cancel out in aggregate analyses that treat all pressure moments as identical.

The finding holds up. Whether I control only for player ranking or include the full set of form variables, the results are consistent: the ATP combined estimate shifts from -0.0325 to -0.0311 and the WTA from -0.0363 to -0.0260 under the reduced specification. The split between break points and tiebreaks is consistent across both tours and stable under the combined robustness check.

Estimating conditional effects via Causal Forest rather than running isolated subgroup regressions mitigates the risk of p-hacking (finding spurious patterns by testing too many hypotheses). Within the ATP, Sinner accounts for 2,169 of 35,635 points; clustered standard errors address variance inflation, though the point estimate may over-index on deep-tournament players. The WTA tiebreak estimate rests on 197 observations, limiting the Causal Forest's sample-splitting stability and making it more fragile than the ATP equivalent. Volunteer-charted datasets skew toward elite broadcast matches, as untelevised courts cannot be recorded. I have no physiological data, and winning a high-leverage point may reflect an unobserved factor affecting both points. I only test immediate point-to-point effects; whether momentum compounds across longer sequences remains an open question. Converting a break point transitions the winner to serving, a position carrying a structural 64% point-win advantage. That the negative effect persists despite this tailwind suggests a drag strong enough to outweigh the serving advantage, though psychological and strategic mechanisms cannot be fully separated here. Future research might employ Monte Carlo simulations of rank-weighted random sequences to establish whether the CUSUM oscillations fall within natural variance.

But the picture is clearer than it has ever been at this scale. In tennis, researchers have long debated whether the hot hand exists. The evidence suggests they may have been asking too broad a question. Momentum appears to exist in tiebreaks. It runs in reverse at break points. And because break points happen roughly four times more often than tiebreaks at Grand Slams, the positive effect can be obscured in pooled aggregate analyses.

The next time a commentator says Alcaraz has the momentum after converting a break point, the data suggests caution. If he just won a tiebreak point, they might actually be onto something.
